summary: Hancock concurs that the proposed ORV management policy—closing some public lands and opening others with controls—is consistent with responsible stewardship of natural resources and recreation interests. However, she raises several concerns: the noise criterion is too vague, issuing permits for ORV races and events is unwise (better left to the private sector), and monitoring must be built into any designation system. She also notes that New Hampshire cannot fully endorse the policy until the Department of Agriculture issues its own statement covering the White Mountain National Forest, and that any specific designation plans for federal lands within New Hampshire must be open to state evaluation.

statement.text:
INTER-DEPARTMENT COMMUNICATION
JUL 6 572
FROM Mary Louise Hancock, Director
DATE June 29, 1972
AT (DAFICE) State Planning
SUBJECT Draft Environmental Statement, Department of Interior, regarding the Use of Qff - Road Vehicles
To Alexander M. Taft, Director Comprehensive Planning
Members of my staff have reviewed the draft environmental statement, prepared by the Department of Interior, entitled "Departmental Implementation of Executive Order 11544 Pertaining to Use of Off-Road Vehicles on the Public Lands."
We concur that the proposed management policy which would close some public lands to the use of off-road vehicles (ORV) and open others with controls, is consistent with the Department's responsibilities to meet the outdoor recreation interests of the public while maintaining the long-term stewardship for the soil, water, mineral, wildlife, vegetative, and natural and historic resources of the Nation.
The designation of areas closed to ORV use based on physical and biological impacts makes a great deal of sense. Predictions of impacts are not in themselves sufficient. Monitoring of designated use areas must be provided for, and management must be sufficiently flexible to allow changes based on the results of monitoring.
We question the wisdom of issuing permits for the use of public lands as sites for ORV races, rallies, meets, etc. Such intensive use can be better provided by the private sector.
The issue of excessive noise poses some difficult problems. First, there is the definitional problem. No attempt is made to specify what decibel level is considered to be acceptable. Second, the Operating Criteria include a clause that "...an ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The environmental impact of that management policy states in part that "...most motorized ORV are noisy in excess of acceptable levels." Logic demands, therefore, that most motorized ORV shall not be permitted on Interior lands. Obviously, the criterion of "excessive noise" is too vague to be of any use.
Since the State of New Hampshire will be affected greatly by policies yet to be promulgated by the Department of Agriculture through its large White Mountain Muticaul Forest, we cannot at this time be certain that we fully endorse the policy and projected impact set forth by Interior. This can better be ascertained after we have had an opportunity to review Agriculture's 102 Statement.
We wish to emphasize that New Hampshire feels a need to evaluate any specific plans for designating use and non-use areas on Federal lands within the State. The evaluation of a national policy involving lands of great diversity is necessary but not sufficient for an adequate environmental assessment.
MLH: Imd
